strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem—moving from reactive, iterative safety patching to a unified online self-play loop where attacker and defender co-evolve—and the framing as a two-player zero-sum game is well motivated.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: six baselines/ablations (Attacker-Only, Defender-Only, ±SFT, ±Hidden CoT), 8 training runs per method with 95% confidence intervals and bootstrapped checkpoint distributions (Figures 3-4), and a broad benchmark suite covering harmful refusal, over-refusal/benign compliance, and general capability (Table 1 and 2).

The ablation studies are informative: Hidden CoT's effect on over-refusal (WJB:Benign 0.806 vs 0.470 for No-CoT) and the diversity analysis (Self-BLEU, SBERT, t-SNE/DBSCAN clustering, plus a holdout diversity check in B.6) give evidence beyond headline ASR numbers.
Reproducibility materials are strong: full instruction/reward templates, self-distillation pipeline (B.4.2), hyperparameters, and compute details (B.4.3) are provided.

The paper is candid about limitations (single model family, single-turn only, 'active backdoor' risk of retaining attack capability) and includes a serious broader-impact and safeguards discussion (Appendices C, D), including the interesting emergent attacker-refusal phenomenon (D.2).
weaknesses: The 'theoretical safety guarantee' (Theorem 1) is essentially a restatement of the reward structure: given that harmful responses score -1 and the always-refusing defender scores >= 0, a Nash equilibrium defender cannot leave an unsafe response. The proof is a short contradiction argument that adds little beyond a well-known minimax property, and it does not apply to the actual training objective, which departs from the zero-sum game via asymmetric reward shaping terms (refusal, format, revision-faithfulness rewards). The paper leans on this result rhetorically ('the end-point of our proposed training procedure is a fully secure LLM'), which is not warranted.

There is a judge-evaluation circularity concern: WildGuard-7B serves as the reward model during training AND the WildGuard evaluation suite (WG:Test) is a primary safety benchmark where the method shows its best result (0.138 ASR). RL training directly optimizes against this judge's labels, so gains on that benchmark may partially reflect judge overfitting rather than true robustness; the paper does not ablate the judge or evaluate with a held-out independent judge.

The headline improvements are relative to the abliterated baseline and their own Defender-Only baselines, not to the official safety-aligned Llama-3.1-8B-IT. Against that model, Self-Play+SFT is mixed (e.g., worse WJB adv harm ASR 0.240 vs 0.063, worse OR-Bench XSTest benign compliance 0.806/0.920 vs 0.984/0.940), so the claim of advancing state-of-the-art safety alignment should be tempered.

General-capability retention is a real cost: without the auxiliary SFT component, AlpacaEval-2 LC winrate drops from 19.22 to 10.51 and average length collapses (2333 to 582), and the final method (16.34) still trails the original model. The 'minimal to none capability degradation' claim in §6.1 overstates this; the SFT regularizer is doing substantial work.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing self-play/adversarial-coevolution work (Perez et al. red-teaming, SPAG, SPPO, SPIN, eva, DuoGuard, Ma et al.); the contribution is 'doing it fully online with full-parameter updates' plus Hidden CoT, which is a reasonable but not fundamental advance, and the 'first end-to-end online MARL' claim is largely an engineering distinction.

Generalization evidence is thin: results are on a single 8B model family, single-turn only, with training and evaluation heavily drawn from the WildJailBreak ecosystem (also used for seeds, SFT prompts, and evaluation), raising train/eval leakage-style concerns; the limitations section acknowledges some of this.

Presentation issues remain: 'Limitaions' typo, 'Boarder Impact' heading, duplicate citations ([5]/[7], [6]/[12], [47]/[11]), and some claims in the abstract (e.g., '+65.5% on WildJailBreak') are framed in ways that could mislead without the Defender-Only context.

strengths: The core idea of fully online, end-to-end self-play MARL for safety alignment (attacker and defender co-evolving within a single RL loop) is well-motivated and addresses a genuine limitation of the prevailing sequential red-team-then-patch paradigm.

The empirical evaluation is broad: six training variants, multiple safety benchmarks spanning harmful refusal and benign compliance, general capability benchmarks, and diversity metrics (Self-BLEU, SBERT) computed both during training and on a holdout set (B.6), with 8 runs and 95% confidence intervals.

The paper is commendably transparent about limitations: single model family, single-turn setting, the 'active backdoor' risk of retaining attacker capability, and an appendix (D) discussing external safeguards and an emergent internal safeguard phenomenon.
Training infrastructure details (OpenRLHF, Re++, hyperparameters, compute budget) and instruction templates are provided in sufficient detail to support approximate reproducibility.

The co-evolution dynamics analysis (RQ4, Figure 3) provides genuine insight, e.g., showing that attacker-only training degrades revision faithfulness (~50%) due to reward hacking, and that Defender-Only's near-perfect convergence against static attacks does not transfer to held-out robustness.
weaknesses: The 'theoretical safety guarantee' (Theorem 1) is substantially oversold. The result is close to circular: it assumes refusals receive zero reward and unsafe responses receive -1, from which NE safety follows almost by definition. More importantly, the actually implemented reward (Section 4.1) contradicts the theorem's assumptions—it adds refusal sub-rewards that penalize blanket refusal, plus format and revision shaping terms, and the defender is optimized jointly with SFT. Thus the theory neither motivates nor applies to the method as deployed, yet the abstract and Section 3 repeatedly lean on it as a principled foundation.

There is a serious judge-circularity concern: WildGuard-7B serves as both the training reward model and a primary evaluation suite (WG:Test, and the WildJailBreak pipeline). The defender is explicitly optimized to satisfy this classifier, so strong WG numbers may partly reflect classifier-specific overfitting rather than genuine safety. No human evaluation or independent judge (e.g., a different classifier family or human annotation of a subsample) is reported to rule this out.

The central claim of 'minimal to none capability degradation' is not well supported by Table 2: with SFT, IFEval drops from 0.778/0.823 to 0.592/0.693 and AlpacaEval-2 LC winrate falls from 25.14 to 16.34 versus the official Llama-3.1-8B-IT; without SFT, average response length collapses from 2069 to 582 tokens, suggesting degenerate verbosity behavior. These are substantial degradations, not 'minimal.'

Several headline comparisons are less favorable than the text implies. On benign compliance, Self-Play + SFT (0.806 WJB adv benign, 0.920 XSTest vani benign) is outperformed by Defender-Only + SFT (0.871, 0.932) and even by the original abliterated baseline (0.992, 0.988); the over-refusal mitigation attributed to Hidden CoT is measured against a weak No-CoT ablation rather than strong static baselines.

Generality is thin: all experiments use a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-abliterated), an unusual and non-standard starting checkpoint, single-turn interactions only, and safety training/evaluation drawn largely from the same WildJailBreak distribution, raising train-eval overlap concerns.

The abstract's quantified claims (+21.8% SBERT diversity, +65.5% WildJailBreak robustness, +45.3% from Hidden CoT) are difficult to trace to the reported tables/figures and lack clear baselines or significance tests, weakening the evidential chain.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: typos ('Limitaions', 'Boarder Impact', 'tempearture'), duplicated references ([5]/[7], [6]/[12], [11]/[47]), a malformed citation list ('[4, 6, 6, 36, 46-57]'), and heavy reliance on relegated figures (t-SNE, DBSCAN) that are suggestive rather than quantitative.

The 'first end-to-end online MARL framework for full-parameter LM safety training' novelty claim is aggressively scoped; the delta over prior co-evolution work (DuoGuard, Ma et al.) amounts mainly to online RL and hidden CoT, and the incremental contribution of hidden CoT—an established reasoning-template technique—is modest.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem—moving from reactive safety patching to co-evolutionary attacker/defender training—and the framing of safety alignment as a two-player zero-sum self-play game is intuitive and well-motivated.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 8 training runs with 95% confidence intervals, multiple ablations (Self-Play, No-CoT, ±SFT, Attacker-Only, Defender-Only), safety benchmarks spanning several suites, general-capability benchmarks to check for degradation, and a holdout-set diversity analysis (Appendix B.6) that validates the diversity claims.

Transparent and detailed reproducibility information: full instruction templates, reward definitions, dataset composition, hyperparameters, and compute footprint are provided, which others can realistically build on.
The Hidden CoT mechanism is a interesting design point with a clear ablation showing it substantially improves benign compliance (0.806 vs 0.470 ASR on WJB:Benign) relative to no-CoT training.

Honest limitations section (single model family, single-turn only, backdoor risk) plus a thoughtful safeguards appendix (D.1) discussing external protections for released adversarially-trained checkpoints.
The dynamics analysis (RQ4, Figure 3) is informative—it shows attacker-only training degenerates in revision faithfulness (~50%), a concrete failure mode supporting the co-evolution argument.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is overstated and nearly tautological. Theorem 1's 'safety guarantee' follows directly from assuming that blanket refusal earns non-negative reward; any policy achieving this guarantee trivially exists (the refuser), so the result does not substantiate that self-play co-evolution is needed. Moreover, the actual reward used in training (composite shaped rewards, plus auxiliary SFT) departs from the clean zero-sum [−1,1] game assumed in the theorem, so the guarantee does not strictly apply to the deployed method. The paper should soften these claims.

Potential circularity between training reward and evaluation: WildGuard-7B supplies the game rewards during training (prompt harmfulness, response harmfulness, refusal), and the evaluation suite is built around WildGuard/WildJailBreak-derived benchmarks, including the headline WG:Test and WJB numbers. This risks overestimating true safety gains; there is no human evaluation or independent judge (e.g., LlamaGuard-only results reported separately) to break the tie.

Training uses WildJailBreak vanilla prompts and the main improvement is largest on WJB adv. harm (0.240 vs 0.432 for Defender-Only+SFT), raising distribution-overlap concerns for the flagship result; gains on out-of-suite benchmarks (HarmBench adv. harm: 0.396 vs 0.452; OR-Bench: 0.221 vs 0.260) are modest, and the method is not clearly better than the official Llama-3.1-8B-IT on several hard benchmarks (e.g., 0.396 vs 0.533 on HarmBench adv. harm).

Starting from an 'abliterated' (deliberately de-aligned) checkpoint is a consequential methodological choice: it is convenient but introduces a dual-use artifact whose release needs careful justification, and the claim that safety gains are 'competitive with or superior to' the officially aligned model is not consistently supported by Table 1 (e.g., DAN 0.396 vs 0.675 favors the method, but HarmBench adv. harm 0.533 for the official model vs 0.396 — wait, this actually favors the method; however XSTest benign compliance drops to 0.806 vs 0.984, an over-refusal trade-off that is under-discussed).

Some presentation sloppiness undermines confidence: duplicated references ([5]=[7], [6]=[12]), typos ('Limitaions', 'Boarder Impact', 'tempearture', 'simutaneously'), and the abstract's '+65.5% on WildJailBreak' figure is not directly traceable to the tables presented.

Generality is limited: single model family (Llama-3.1-8B), single-turn only, and the theoretical framework's connection to the empirical setup is loose (shaped rewards, reward hacking partially mitigated by the revision-faithfulness term rather than by the game itself).

strengths: The core idea — casting safety alignment as an online, two-player zero-sum self-play game where a single LM alternates attacker/defender roles with hidden chain-of-thought — is compelling, clearly motivated by the reactive attacker-then-patch mismatch in prior red-teaming pipelines, and represents the first fully online, full-parameter MARL framework for LLM safety (vs. offline/LoRA/quantized predecessors like DuoGuard, SPAG).

The empirical evaluation is thorough: safety is assessed across many benchmarks (WildGuardTest, WildJailBreak, HarmBench, DAN, OR-Bench, XSTest, StrongReject in the appendix) covering both harmful refusal and benign compliance (over-refusal), plus general capability benchmarks (AlpacaEval-2, IFEval, MMLU, GPQA, etc.), with 8-run bootstrapped confidence distributions (Fig. 4) rather than single checkpoints.

The paper does not cherry-pick an easy story: it honestly reports that Self-Play (No CoT) achieves near-perfect safety only via excessive refusal (WJB benign ASR 0.470), that standalone Self-Play degrades AlpacaEval-2, and that Defender-Only converges to better in-game winrates without transferring to real robustness — these observations give genuine insight into the safety-vs-helpfulness trade-off and the role of CoT.

Reward design is carefully thought out (game outcome rewards plus shaping terms for CoT format, revision faithfulness, refusal calibration), benign seed prompts are used to combat over-refusal, and implementation details (OpenRLHF/Re++, hyperparameters, 4×A100 compute budget, ~10-15h per run) are sufficient for reasonable reproducibility.

Limitations and ethics are treated seriously and honestly: single model family in the main text, single-turn focus, dual-use/active-backdoor risk from retaining attack capability, and concrete safeguards (E.1), plus an emergent attacker-refusal phenomenon analyzed transparently (E.2). Preliminary results on Qwen-2.5 3B/7B/14B and multi-turn transfer (X-Teaming) partially address generalization concerns.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) is near-vacuous and oversold. It essentially proves that if an 'always-refuse' defender is a feasible deviation receiving reward ≥ 0, then a Nash defender cannot ever be unsafe (reward −1) — a direct consequence of the payoff structure, contingent on assuming the reward model perfectly separates safe/unsafe and that refusal yields exactly zero reward. The abstract's claim of a 'theoretical safety guarantee' that the defender 'will reliably produce safe responses to any adversarial input' is only as strong as the reward model, and the trained system's actual rewards (shaped composite rewards, SFT regularization, KL penalties) diverge substantially from the idealized game, so the connection between theory and practice is weak.

There is a judge–evaluation circularity concern: WildGuard-7B serves as the in-training reward/adjudicator, and the primary safety evaluation suite is the WildGuard family. The attacker is explicitly trained to evade this exact judge, and the defender to satisfy it, so reduced ASR on WG:Test/WJB may partly reflect judge alignment rather than genuine safety gains, and the attacker could be hacking the judge (the paper itself notes Attacker-Only hacks revision faithfulness). Human or independent-judge validation is missing.

The main results are from a single model (Llama-3.1-8B) and an 'abliterated' starting checkpoint — a model with safety alignment deliberately removed — which both complicates comparison to standard practice (all baselines start from this unusual point) and raises its own safety concerns; the broader Qwen/Llama-IT results are labeled preliminary and, notably, are mixed (e.g., on Qwen-3B and Qwen-7B, Self-Play variants are frequently worse than Defender-Only on harmful-refusal ASRs, and Self-Play hurts AlpacaEval-2 substantially on Llama-3.1-8B-IT), which weakens the claimed general superiority of self-play.

Advantages over the best baselines are sometimes modest and inconsistent: Self-Play + SFT beats Defender-Only + SFT on some benchmarks (WG:Test adv harm 0.138 vs 0.251, DAN 0.396 vs 0.432) but is worse or comparable on others (OR-Bench RTA 0.846 vs 0.873; WJB adv benign compliance 0.806 vs 0.894), and no statistical significance tests accompany the headline deltas despite 8-run data being available.

Presentation issues undermine polish: typos ('Limitaions', 'Boarder Impact', 'tempearture', 'simutaneously'), reward terms left with colored highlighting that appears to be leftover review-style annotation, duplicated/near-duplicate references ([5,7], [6,12], [11,47], [22,66]), and a blue 'future work' notice in Appendix A stating the authors 'plan a major revision' — signaling the manuscript is still in flux.

The diversity claim (+21.8% SBERT, +45.3% with hidden CoT) rests on embedding-distribution statistics (t-SNE visuals, Self-BLEU, SBERT similarity) that are indicative but not tied to a measurable downstream outcome (e.g., defender robustness gains from attacking diverse prompts vs. redundant ones), and the reported diversity numbers for the No-CoT variant are absent from the headline comparisons.

The 'fully secure LLM' endpoint framing (§3) overstates what is achievable: NE convergence is neither verified nor guaranteed by the algorithm, and safety as judged by a fallible classifier is not the same as actual harmlessness.

strengths: The core idea of fully online self-play MARL for safety alignment is timely and well-motivated, addressing a genuine limitation of sequential attack/defend pipelines.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the main model: safety is assessed across many benchmarks (HarmBench, WildGuardTest, WildJailBreak, DAN, XSTest, OR-Bench), with general capability checks and an explicit over-refusal/compliance axis.

The paper provides a thoughtful set of ablations (Attacker-Only, Defender-Only, ±SFT, ±Hidden CoT) and interesting dynamics analysis (Figures 3 and 4), including a diversity analysis with both t-SNE visualization and a holdout-set diversity evaluation (§C.6).
Appendices cover implementation details, reward decomposition, prompts, and an honest discussion of emergent attacker-refusal behavior (§E.2) and dual-use risks (§D, §E.1).
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim (Theorem 1) is nearly vacuous. The 'safety guarantee' assumes the reward directly encodes safety (r = -1 iff unsafe, refusal yields ≥ 0), so the theorem essentially restates the reward model's definition of safety as a game-theoretic result. It is also disconnected from the actual training setup, which uses a composite reward (harm, refusal, format, faithfulness shaping terms) rather than the clean zero-sum [-1,1] reward assumed in the proof, and the paper presents no convergence-to-NE evidence. Framing this as a 'safety guarantee that motivates the design' oversells the contribution.

Evaluation appears partially circular: WildGuard-7B is the judge/reward model during training, while safety is evaluated on WildGuard's own evaluation suite (WildGuardTest, WildJailBreak), creating a potential training-evaluation alignment advantage for the proposed method over baselines judged by the same model.

The headline claim of 'minimal to none capability degradation' is not supported by Table 2: relative to the abliterated starting point, AlpacaEval-2 LC winrate drops 19.22 → 16.34 and IFEval drops 0.738/0.823 → 0.592/0.693, a substantial instruction-following loss. Appendix A further admits AlpacaEval-2 drops of ~15-17% on Llama-family models.

The paper is not finished. Appendix A is explicitly labeled preliminary ('As of August 2025... we plan a major revision of this paper based on the updated results'), with mixed and sometimes unfavorable results buried in Tables 3-6 (e.g., Self-play + SFT is notably worse than Self-play alone on several safety metrics for Qwen-7B, and the headline Self-play + SFT gains are not consistently the best across models). This undercuts the generality claims made in the abstract.

Hidden CoT claims are confounded: the No-CoT ablation achieves by far the best safety scores (e.g., 0.006 vs. 0.138 ASR on WG:Test) but poor benign compliance, so the CoT contribution is really about a refusal/compliance trade-off rather than a clean diversity benefit; the causal attribution to 'strategic planning' remains speculative.

Key baselines from the related-work discussion (Rainbow Teaming, SPAG, DuoGuard, Ma et al.) are not empirically compared; the strongest comparator is an internal ablation (Defender-Only + SFT) rather than existing co-evolution methods. Statistical significance is reported only for training curves, not for the main results tables.

Dual-use treatment is thin: the final shared checkpoint retains a capable attack-generation mode ('active backdoor'), and the proposed mitigations (prompt engineering, ethical click-through agreements) are weak relative to the risk, which the paper itself acknowledges only briefly.

Presentation quality is below venue standard: multiple typos ('Limitaions and Future Work', 'Boarder Impact', 'tempearture', 'genereate'), and the methodology section mixes theoretical framing that the experiments do not actually instantiate.

strengths: The core idea is compelling and well-motivated: recasting safety alignment as an online two-player zero-sum self-play game with a shared policy alternating between attacker and defender roles, which directly addresses the reactive patching loop that plagues current safety pipelines. The hidden Chain-of-Thought mechanism (private reasoning withheld from the opponent) is a neat, novel design element for adversarial MARL with LMs.

The empirical evaluation is broad and largely careful: six safety benchmarks spanning harmful refusal and benign compliance, general capability benchmarks (IFEval, AlpacaEval-2, ARC-C, GPQA, MMLU, TruthfulQA, BBH), diversity metrics (Self-BLEU, SBERT), t-SNE/DBSCAN cluster analysis, a holdout-set diversity evaluation (Appendix C.6), and results averaged over 8 checkpoints with 95% CIs (Figure 4).

Ablations are thorough and honest: the paper does not cherry-pick; e.g., it reports that Self-Play (No CoT) achieves the best raw safety numbers but catastrophically over-refuses (WJB:Benign 0.470), and that standalone Self-Play degrades instruction following, motivating the SFT variant.

Appendix A extends experiments to four additional models (Qwen2.5 3B/7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-IT) and adds StrongREJECT and X-Teaming multi-turn transfer results, which substantially mitigate the single-model-family concern.

The limitations section is candid (single-turn focus, single family, 'active backdoor' risk from retaining attack capabilities, emergent attacker refusal in one checkpoint), and Appendix E provides concrete safeguards (external classifiers, ethical use agreements, mitigations for released checkpoints).
weaknesses: Theorem 1 and its proof are essentially trivial and over-sold. The result reduces to: 'at NE the defender is never worse than an always-refusing defender, which earns non-negative reward.' This is a near-immediate observation once the zero-refusal reward convention is assumed, and it critically depends on an assumed perfect reward model. The paper repeatedly frames this as a 'theoretical safety guarantee' and a 'principled route to safer models,' which overstates its content. Moreover, the implemented game deviates substantially from the formalized game (multiple reward shaping terms, refusal sub-rewards, SFT mixing), so the connection between theory and method is loose at best.

Potential circularity between the training judge and the evaluation suite: WildGuard-7B provides the reward labels during RL training, and two of the headline safety benchmarks (WildGuardTest, WildJailBreak partitions) come from the same WildGuard/WildTeam ecosystem. Even with careful construction, ASR improvements on these benchmarks could partially reflect better calibration to the judge's decision boundary rather than genuinely broader robustness. Cross-judge evaluation (e.g., LlamaGuard, StrongREJECT in the main table, human audit of a sample) should be more prominent.

Main-text comparisons are on an abliterated (safety-removed) checkpoint, and the strongest baseline comparisons are muddied by confounds: Defender-Only collapses in response length (607 tokens on AlpacaEval-2) without the SFT data, and the results are mixed rather than dominant — e.g., Defender-Only + SFT beats Self-Play + SFT on OR-Bench RTA (0.873 vs 0.846) and WJB vanilla harm (0.871 vs 0.814). The 'self-play is better' narrative holds on some benchmarks but not uniformly, and the paper does not deeply analyze when/why self-play wins or loses.

The 'first scalable, end-to-end online MARL for LM safety' claim is aggressive given closely related co-evolution work (DuoGuard's two-player RL framework, Ma et al.'s multi-round multi-agent red-teaming games, SPAG, X-Teaming); the distinction reduces mostly to online vs. offline updates, which should be argued more carefully rather than asserted.

General capability degradation is non-trivial: IFEval drops from 0.823/0.850 (baseline instruct) to 0.584-0.693 for all trained variants, and AlpacaEval-2 LC winrate never recovers to the official instruct model (16.34 vs 25.14). 'Minimal to none capability degradation' in the section title is not fully supported by Table 2.

Appendix A admits the manuscript is not in its final state ('plan a major revision of this paper based on the updated results'), which is unusual and complicates assessment of which results the authors themselves consider definitive.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: training details and prompts are given, but there is no explicit statement of code/checkpoint release; released checkpoints would also raise the dual-use concern the paper itself acknowledges (a fine-tuned attack generator). Presentation has noticeable typos ('Limitaions', 'Boarder Impact').
